name: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
title: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
answer: XBRL tagging is the practice of marking up financial statements and disclosures with machine readable tags drawn from a published taxonomy, so that a regulator, an analyst or a downstream system can pull a specific figure without re keying a filing. It sits inside statutory and regulatory reporting, where the tagged document is the filing of record rather than a summary of it. The work covers the primary statements, the notes, and increasingly the narrative sections that carry numeric or date based facts. In practice the scope question is always which taxonomy, which period and which reporting regime apply to the entity in front of you.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack is a taxonomy, a tagging or preparation tool, a validation engine and the regulator's submission gateway. Preparers commonly work in a disclosure management product or an ERP reporting module that exports XBRL, then run the output through the filing system's own checks before submission. The taxonomy itself is versioned, so the same concept can carry different definitions across years and regimes. Nothing here needs a model to run, though tagging tools increasingly suggest concepts as a preparer types.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The preparer maps each reported line to a concept, extends the taxonomy where no standard concept fits, and anchors those extensions so a reader can trace them back to a base element. Calculation and presentation linkbases then assert how the tagged facts relate, and the validator tests those assertions against the arithmetic in the document. Review is a reconciliation exercise: the tagged instance must agree with the human readable filing line for line. Most errors surface as broken calculations, wrong signs, or a fact tagged to a concept that means something subtly different from the label on the page.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Responsibility for a filing sits with the reporting entity and its officers, not with the software vendor or the tagging consultant. Extensions are the main audit and review pressure point, because a custom concept can obscure a figure that a standard one would have exposed. Provenance matters in both directions: the tagged fact must trace to a source document, and any later correction must be reflected in the instance rather than only in the narrative. Internal controls over financial reporting generally extend to the tagging process, and the audit trail for concept choices is part of what gets examined.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Regulators have steadily widened what must be tagged, moving from the primary statements into the notes and toward structured narrative disclosure. That widening raises the cost of taxonomy drift and puts more weight on consistent extension practice across filers. Machine consumption is the point of the exercise, so the practical direction is toward fewer bespoke tags, tighter validation at submission, and comparison tools that read across filings rather than one at a time. For preparers the recurring question is how much of the mapping can be automated without giving up the reconciliation that makes the filing defensible.
